For x≥2, expand the finite Euler product as a product of geometric series:
P(x):=∏p≤x​(1−p1​)−1=∑n≥1p∣n⇒p≤x​​n1​.
(1)
Every integer 1≤n≤x has all its prime factors at most x, so
P(x)≥∑n≤x​n1​.
(2)
The harmonic series diverges, and therefore
p∏​(1−p1​)−1=∞.​
(3)
Suppose instead that ∑p​1/p converged. For 0<t≤1/2,
0≤−log(1−t)−t=∑j≥2​jtj​≤1−tt2​≤2t2.
(4)
Since ∑p​1/p2 converges, this would make
logP(x)=∑p≤x​−log(1−p1​)
(5)
converge to a finite limit, contradicting the divergence of P(x). Hence the Euler proof that the sum of reciprocals of primes diverges gives
p∑​p1​=∞.​

Assume for contradiction that π=a/b with positive integers a,b. Define
Fn​(x)=n!bn​xn(π−x)n=n!1​xn(a−bx)n
(7)
and
In​=∫0π​Fn​(x)sinxdx.
(8)
The coefficient of xn+j in Fn​ is
n!(−1)j​(jn​)an−jbj.
(9)
Consequently every derivative Fn(k)​(0) is an integer: it is zero unless n≤k≤2n, and in that range the factor k!/n! clears the denominator. Since Fn​(π−x)=Fn​(x), every Fn(k)​(π) is also an integer.
Repeated integration by parts, ending when derivatives above degree 2n vanish, gives
In​=∑j=0n​(−1)j(Fn(2j)​(0)+Fn(2j)​(π)).
(10)
Thus In​ is an integer. It is strictly positive because Fn​(x)sinx>0 for 0<x<π.
On the other hand, x(π−x)≤π2/4, so
0<In​≤n!π​(4bπ2​)n.
(11)
The factorial-over-power series implies that the right-hand side tends to zero. For all sufficiently large n this says that the positive integer In​ is less than one, a contradiction. Therefore the Irrationality of pi is established:
π∈/Q.​

a OurBigBook.com
In Diffie-Hellman key exchange, Alice and Bob publicly agree on a cyclic group G=⟨g⟩ in which the discrete logarithm problem is believed hard. Alice chooses a secret a and sends A=ga; Bob chooses a secret b and sends B=gb. They independently compute
Ba=(gb)a=gab=(ga)b=Ab.
(13)
Thus
K=gab​
(14)
is their shared key. A passive eavesdropper sees g,ga,gb but is believed unable to compute gab efficiently; this is the computational Diffie--Hellman assumption. The basic protocol does not authenticate the participants and is therefore vulnerable to a man-in-the-middle attack unless the exchanged values are authenticated.

b

Words: 97 Articles: 1
3G OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 97
b OurBigBook.com
No. The procedure exposes a square-root oracle for the Rabin cryptosystem. The verifier chooses m, sends r=m2modN, and receives another square root m1​. If
m1​≡±m(modN),
(15)
then the factorization from distinct square roots modulo a semiprime gives
gcd(m−m1​,N) is a nontrivial factor of N.​
(16)
For a product of two odd primes, a square normally has four roots, and a returned root lies outside the pair {±m} with probability about 1/2. Repeating chosen-square challenges therefore factors N with overwhelming probability. The attacker can then compute square roots and impersonate Alice. This is the chosen-square attack on Rabin authentication, so the proposed protocol is insecure.

Let
L1​={wn:w∈{a,b}∗, n≥2}.
(17)
Intersect it with the regular language
R=a+ba+b.
(18)
Every word of R contains exactly two copies of b. If it is a proper power, its exponent must therefore be two and its root must contain one b. Hence
L1​∩R={ambamb:m≥1}.
(19)
This language is not regular: if p were a pumping length, pumping any nonempty substring among the first p copies of a in apbapb would change only its first a-block. Since regular languages are closed under intersection,
L1​ is not regular.​

Solution
Words: 62
ii OurBigBook.com
This language is recognized by the parity-counting deterministic finite automaton with four states
Q={(pb​,pc​):pb​,pc​∈Z2​}.
(21)
The initial state is (0,0) and the only accepting state is (1,0). Reading a leaves the state unchanged, reading b toggles pb​, and reading c toggles pc​. The state therefore records exactly the parities of the numbers of b's and c's. Thus
the language is regular.​
(22)

Solution
Words: 77
iii OurBigBook.com
Use the bounded-run deterministic finite automaton with states
q0​,q1​,…,q7​,qdead​.
(23)
State qj​ records that the current suffix consists of exactly j consecutive zeros. Every q0​,…,q7​ is accepting; qdead​ is rejecting. Reading 1 sends every accepting state to q0​, while reading 0 sends qj​ to qj+1​ for j<7 and sends q7​ to qdead​. The dead state loops on both symbols. This finite automaton accepts exactly the words with no run of eight zeros, so
the language is regular.​
(24)

Solution

Words: 166
b OurBigBook.com
Let K⊆N be the undecidable set denoted K in the question. The language satisfies the pumping lemma for regular languages with pumping length one. For any nonempty s∈L, write s=xyz with x=ε, y its first symbol, and z the remaining suffix.
If s∈b∗, then xyiz∈b∗ for every i≥0. Otherwise s=wabn for some n∈K. If the chosen first symbol lies in w, pumping it preserves the same final suffix abn. If w=ε, then s=abn: pumping down gives bn∈b∗, while every positive pump gives aibn and all but its last a can be absorbed into w. Thus every sufficiently long word has a valid pumping decomposition.
Nevertheless, if L were regular language, closure under intersection would make
L∩ab∗={abn:n∈K}
(25)
regular. A finite automaton deciding this unary language would decide whether n∈K by running it on abn, contradicting the halting problem. Therefore
L satisfies the pumping lemma but is not regular.​
(26)
This is a nonregular language satisfying the pumping lemma.

Solution

Words: 185
5J OurBigBook.com
A (1−α) prediction interval is a pair of statistics L(Y),U(Y) such that, for every β and σ2>0, an independent future response Y∗ at the specified input satisfies
Prβ,σ2​{L(Y)≤Y∗≤U(Y)}=1−α.
(27)
In the normal linear model, assume X has full column rank and write
β​=(XTX)−1XTy,s2=n−p∥y−Xβ​∥22​​.
(28)
For a new observation
Y∗=x∗Tβ+ε∗,ε∗∼N(0,σ2),
(29)
independent of the training sample, the prediction error is
Y∗−x∗Tβ​=ε∗−x∗T(β​−β).
(30)
The two terms on the right are independent centered normal random variables, while
Var(β​)=σ2(XTX)−1.
(31)
Consequently, with the new-point regression leverage
h∗=x∗T(XTX)−1x∗,
(32)
we have
σ1+h∗​Y∗−x∗Tβ​​∼N(0,1).
(33)
The assumption in the question gives
σ2(n−p)s2​=σ2∥y−Xβ​∥22​​∼χn−p2​.
(34)
This variable is independent of β​; it is also independent of the new error ε∗. Therefore it is independent of the standardized prediction error, and the defining normal-over-chi-square representation of Student's t-distribution gives
s1+h∗​Y∗−x∗Tβ​​∼tn−p​.
(35)
If tn−p,1−α/2​ is the corresponding upper quantile, symmetry yields
Pr(​s1+h∗​Y∗−x∗Tβ​​​≤tn−p,1−α/2​)=1−α.
(36)
Solving these inequalities for Y∗ proves that the prediction interval in a normal linear model is
x∗Tβ​±tn−p,1−α/2​s1+x∗T(XTX)−1x∗​.​
(37)
Its center and endpoints depend only on the observed data and x∗, and the pivotal calculation proves the required coverage uniformly in the unknown β and σ2.

Put x(t)=1+u(t). Retaining terms linear in u gives
u′(t)=α[u(t)−2u(t−T)].
(38)
The exponential ansatz u=eλt gives the characteristic equation of a delay differential equation
λ=α(1−2e−λT).
(39)
At T=0 its root is λ=−α, and the remaining delay roots lie far in the left half-plane, so the equilibrium is stable for sufficiently small T.
A stability change can first occur when λ=iω. Separating real and imaginary parts gives
cos(ωT)=21​,ω=2αsin(ωT).
(40)
For the first positive crossing, ωT=π/3 and ω=3​α. Thus
Tc​=33​απ​.​
(41)
All positive-frequency crossings have ωT=π/3+2πk, so there is no earlier imaginary-axis crossing. Implicit differentiation of
F(λ,T)=λ−α+2αe−λT=0
(42)
gives, with q=αTc​,
RedTdλ​=(1−q)2+3q23α2​>0,
(43)
so the conjugate pair crosses into the right half-plane as T increases. Therefore the stability threshold for delayed quadratic crowding is
x=1 is stable for 0≤T<Tc​ and loses stability at T=Tc​.​

(48)
and take the branch cut [−1,1]. On C∖[−1,1], choose the analytic branch of a square root whose upper boundary value is
s(x+i0)=+1−x2​,−1<x<1.
(49)
Its lower boundary value is s(x−i0)=−1−x2​. This fixes the integrand to be +1 at 0+ as required.
For 0≤argz≤π, start at 0+ and use any path to z lying above the cut; path deformations within that region do not alter the integral by the Cauchy integral theorem. For π<argz<2π, start in the same way, continue counterclockwise around the branch point −1 from the upper bank to the lower bank, and then continue to z through the lower half-plane. This second prescription is the continuation obtained as argz increases through π.

Start with the germ w=Arcsin(z) selected in part (a) and continue it along paths in C∖{−1,1}. At the two branch points,
Arcsin(1)=2π​,Arcsin(−1)=−2π​.
(50)
The monodromy reflection at a square-root branch point therefore shows that continuation once around 1 sends w to π−w, while continuation once around −1 sends it to −π−w. Composing these reflections produces every translation by an even multiple of π. Hence the branches of the complex inverse sine are
arcsin(z)=nπ+(−1)nArcsin(z),n∈Z.​

1−t2​∼−it,1−t2​1​∼ti​.
(52)
The change in the primitive is consequently
limR→∞​∮∣t∣=R​1−t2​dt​=∮ti​dt=−2π.

Equivalently, this is the composition of the two reflections described by the monodromy of the complex inverse sine. Thus, for this orientation,
arcsin(e2πiz)=Arcsin(z)−2π.​

The reverse orientation gives Arcsin(z)+2π. Both continued values invert the same z, so sin(w−2π)=sinw on an open set of inverse values. The identity theorem extends this equality to every w∈C, proving the periodicity of the complex sine:

Let e1​,e2​,e3​ be a principal body frame, let I1​,I2​,I3​ be the corresponding principal moments of inertia, and write the angular velocity as ω=∑i​ωi​ei​. The body-frame components of the angular momentum are
L=∑i=13​Ii​ωi​ei​.
(56)
No external torque acts, so L is constant in the fixed space frame. Since a body-fixed basis vector satisfies e˙i​=ω×ei​,
0=(dtdL​)space​=(dtdL​)body​+ω×L.
(57)
Taking body-frame components gives the Euler equations for a torque-free rigid body:
I1​ω˙1​I2​ω˙2​I3​ω˙3​​=(I2​−I3​)ω2​ω3​,=(I3​−I1​)ω3​ω1​,=(I1​−I2​)ω1​ω2​.​​
(58)

Multiply the three Euler equations for a torque-free rigid body by ω1​,ω2​,ω3​ and add. The cubic terms cancel, giving conservation of the rotational kinetic energy
E=21​(I1​ω12​+I2​ω22​+I3​ω32​).​
(59)
Instead multiply the equations by I1​ω1​,I2​ω2​,I3​ω3​ and add. The cubic terms again cancel, giving
L2=I12​ω12​+I22​ω22​+I32​ω32​,​
(60)
the squared magnitude of the conserved angular momentum. For an asymmetric body these two quadratic forms are not proportional, so the torque-free rigid-body invariants are independent.

First consider rotation predominantly about the third principal axis, writing ω3​=Ω+O(ω12​+ω22​). To first order the third Euler equation gives Ω˙=0, while the transverse components satisfy
ω˙1​=I1​I2​−I3​​Ωω2​,ω˙2​=I2​I3​−I1​​Ωω1​.
(61)
Therefore
ω¨1​=−Ω2I1​I2​(I3​−I2​)(I3​−I1​)​ω1​,
(62)
and the same equation holds for ω2​.
Order the principal moments as I1​<I2​<I3​. The coefficient above is negative, so perturbations about axis three oscillate and remain bounded. Cyclically applying the same linear stability of principal-axis rotation calculation about axis one gives
ω¨2​=−Ω2I2​I3​(I2​−I1​)(I3​−I1​)​ω2​,
(63)
so that rotation is also stable. About axis two, however,
ω¨1​=+Ω2I1​I3​(I2​−I1​)(I3​−I2​)​ω1​,
(64)
which has an exponentially growing solution. Thus the intermediate axis theorem gives
rotation about the smallest and largest inertia axes is stable, while rotation about the intermediate axis is unstable.​
(65)

For a relativistic species the supplied relation P=ϵ/3 makes its entropy density proportional to T3. The fermion-to-boson thermal integral ratio gives the factor 7/8 for each fermionic degree of freedom, so the electromagnetic plasma immediately before electron-positron annihilation in cosmology has
g∗s,before​=gγ​+87​(ge−​+ge+​)=2+87​(2+2)=211​.
(66)
After annihilation only the two photon polarizations remain, so g∗s,after​=2.
The neutrinos have already undergone neutrino decoupling. They therefore receive none of the electron-positron entropy and cool as Tν​∝a−1. In the still-coupled electromagnetic plasma, cosmological entropy conservation gives g∗s​Tγ3​a3=constant. If Td​ and ad​ denote the common temperature and scale factor just before annihilation, then at a later scale factor a,
2Tγ3​a3=211​Td3​ad3​,Tν3​a3=Td3​ad3​.
(67)
Dividing gives the Cosmic neutrino background temperature ratio
Tγ​Tν​​=(114​)1/3.​
(68)

The multiplicative order of α modulo N is the least positive integer r such that
αr≡1(modN).
(69)
It exists because α and N are coprime integers.
Suppose that r is even and
αr/2≡−1(modN).
(70)
The minimality of r also gives αr/2≡1(modN). Since
(αr/2−1)(αr/2+1)=αr−1≡0(modN),
(71)
the factor extraction from an even modular order yields
gcd(αr/2−1,N)​
(72)
as a nontrivial factor of N; equivalently one may also compute gcd(αr/2+1,N). Thus the required conditions are that r be even and that αr/2≡−1(modN).

A Lagrange top is a rigid body that is symmetric about a principal axis, has a point on that axis fixed in space, and has its center of mass on the same axis while gravity acts uniformly. Here I1​=I2​ is the transverse principal moment of inertia about the fixed point, I3​ is the moment about the symmetry axis, M is the total mass, and l is the distance from the fixed point to the center of mass.
The Euler angles for a symmetric top use θ for inclination, ϕ for precession, and ψ for spin about the body axis. Since ψ is a cyclic coordinate, its generalized momentum
pψ​=I3​(ψ˙​+ϕ˙​cosθ)​
(139)

pϕ​=I1​ϕ˙​sin2θ+pψ​cosθ​

E=21​I1​(θ˙2+ϕ˙​2sin2θ)+2I3​pψ2​​+Mglcosθ.​

We next prove the square of an infinite cardinal. Suppose otherwise and let κ be the least infinite cardinal for which κ2>κ. Well-order κ×κ by increasing

Recursively assign to each pair the least ordinal below κ not already assigned to one of its predecessors. Such an ordinal always exists by the preceding bound, so this constructs an injection κ×κ→κ. The map α↦(α,0) gives the reverse injection, and the Cantor-Schröder-Bernstein theorem yields

A compact topological group is a group G equipped with a compact Hausdorff topology for which multiplication G×G→G and inversion G→G are continuous.
The special unitary group is
SU(n)={U∈Mn​(C):U∗U=I, detU=1}.
(182)
It is closed in the finite-dimensional real vector space Mn​(C) because the equations U∗U=I and detU=1 are closed conditions. It is bounded because every column of a unitary matrix has norm one. The Heine-Borel theorem therefore makes it compact. Matrix multiplication is continuous, and inversion is continuous because U−1=U∗. Hence SU(n) is a compact topological group.

In the one-period building block of the Cox--Ross--Rubinstein model, the money-market account grows by a deterministic factor R>0, while the stock grows independently at each time by
Yt​={U,D,​up,down,​0<D<U.
(315)
Thus St0​=RtS00​ and St1​=S01​∏j=1t​Yj​. Equivalently, the discounted stock has multipliers u=U/R and d=D/R.
The model has no arbitrage precisely when the risk-free return lies strictly between the stock returns:
D<R<U,equivalentlyd<1<u.​
(316)
Indeed, failure of either strict inequality gives a one-period arbitrage, while under the strict inequalities the probability
q=Q(Yt​=U)=U−DR−D​=u−d1−d​​
(317)
lies in (0,1). Taking the moves independent under Q with up probability q makes the discounted stock a martingale, since qu+(1−q)d=1. This is the unique Risk-neutral probability in the Cox--Ross--Rubinstein model, hence the unique equivalent martingale measure.

The two parallel-spin states are already eigenvectors. Diagonalizing the central block gives the four energy eigenvalues
E↑↑​=E↓↓​=4αℏ2​,E±​=−4αℏ2​±B2ℏ2+4α2ℏ4​​.​
(362)
This is the spectrum of the Two-spin Heisenberg Hamiltonian in an opposing longitudinal field.
The asserted ground-state ordering requires the antiferromagnetic case α>0. As B→0,
E−​=−43αℏ2​,E+​=E↑↑​=E↓↓​=4αℏ2​.
(363)
The corresponding state at E−​ is the unique spin-one-half singlet state

The Hamiltonian then has rotational symmetry, so energy depends only on the total-spin sector. The singlet has total spin s=0 and multiplicity one; the triplet has s=1 and multiplicity 2s+1=3. This rotational symmetry explains why the triplet energy eigenspace has dimension three.

Landau theory represents the appropriate thermodynamic potential as an analytic function of a small order parameter, retaining every low-order term allowed by the system's symmetry. At fixed control parameters, the equilibrium phase is the global minimum of the Landau free energy; local minima describe metastable phases. A continuous phase transition occurs when a minimum changes continuously and loses stability, whereas a first-order phase transition occurs when distinct minima exchange global stability.
For
G(ϕ)=41​ϕ4+21​εϕ2,
(383)
the stationary points satisfy
G′(ϕ)=ϕ(ϕ2+ε)=0.
(384)
If ε>0, ϕ=0 is the unique minimum. If ε<0, ϕ=0 is a maximum and the two degenerate minima are
ϕ±​=±−ε​,G(ϕ±​)=−4ε2​.
(385)
Thus the reflection symmetry ϕ↦−ϕ is spontaneously broken below ε=0, and
the transition at ε=0 is continuous, with ∣ϕ∣∼(−ε)1/2.​
(386)

For the sextic even Landau potential
G(ϕ)=61​ϕ6+41​gϕ4+21​εϕ2,
(387)
put q=ϕ2. The stationary-point equation is
G′(ϕ)=ϕ(q2+gq+ε)=0,
(388)
so the nonzero stationary points have
q±​=2−g±g2−4ε​​.
(389)
At such a point, ε=−q2−gq, and hence
G=−31​q3−41​gq2=−q2(3q​+4g​).
(390)
A first-order transition occurs when a nonzero minimum has the same free energy as the disordered minimum G(0)=0. Therefore
q=−43g​,ε=163g2​,g<0.​
(391)
At g=0,ε=0, the first-order line meets the continuous line and forms the tricritical point. For g>0, the transition at ε=0 is continuous.
For g<0, the disordered state ϕ=0 is a local minimum when ε>0 and loses stability at the disordered spinodal point ε=0. The ordered minima exist while
g2−4ε≥0,
(392)
and merge with the intervening maxima at the ordered spinodal ε=g2/4. Consequently the two spinodals enclose a region of metastability. If increasing ε corresponds to heating, the ordered phase can persist above the coexistence curve throughout
superheating:g<0,163g2​<ε<4g2​,​
(393)
while the disordered phase can persist below it throughout
supercooling:g<0,0<ε<163g2​.​
(394)

The source-free Maxwell equations in a linear medium are
∇⋅D=0,∇⋅B=0,∇×E=−∂t∂B​,∇×H=∂t∂D​.​
(395)
Here the constitutive relations are D=εE and B=μH.
Substitution of the sinusoidal plane waves into the two divergence equations gives the transversality of an electromagnetic plane wave,
k⋅E0​=0,k⋅B0​=0.
(396)
Faraday's law and the Ampère-Maxwell equation give, respectively,
k×E0​=ωB0​,k×B0​=−μεωE0​.
(397)
Taking k× the first equation and using transversality yields
−k2E0​=−μεω2E0​.
(398)
Thus a nonzero plane electromagnetic wave in a linear medium must satisfy
k2=μεω2,B0​=ωk×E0​​,vph​=kω​=με​1​.​
(399)
In particular, E0​, B0​, and k are mutually orthogonal, with ∣B0​∣=με​∣E0​∣.
Take the interface to be x=0 and the plane of incidence to be the xy-plane. The incident, reflected, and transmitted wavevectors may be written
kI​kR​kT​​=k−​(cosθI​,sinθI​,0),=k−​(−cosθR​,sinθR​,0),=k+​(cosθT​,sinθT​,0).​
(400)
The phase matching at a planar wave interface requires one common angular frequency and one common tangential wavevector:
k−​sinθI​=k−​sinθR​=k+​sinθT​.
(401)
Since k±​=ωε±​μ​=n±​ω/c, this gives the Snell law for electromagnetic waves,
θR​=θI​,n−​sinθI​=n+​sinθT​.​
(402)
For the final polarization, take the signed electric amplitudes along z. The dielectric-interface boundary conditions require continuity of tangential E and H. Since
H=μωk×E​,
(403)
their z- and y-components give
EI​+ER​=ET​,
(404)
and
k−​cosθI​(EI​−ER​)=k+​cosθT​ET​.
(405)
Eliminating EI​ yields
ET​ER​​=21​(1−k−​cosθI​k+​cosθT​​).
(406)
Using θR​=θI​ and Snell's law,
k−​cosθI​k+​cosθT​​=sinθT​cosθR​sinθR​cosθT​​=tanθT​tanθR​​.
(407)
Therefore the reflected-to-transmitted transverse-electric amplitude ratio is
∣ET​∣∣ER​∣​=21​(1−tanθT​tanθR​​),​
(408)
with the polarization directions chosen so that the displayed signed factor is nonnegative; otherwise its absolute value gives the magnitude ratio.

Let u be the Stokes flow and let v be any other admissible incompressible flow with the same no-slip boundary condition on the sphere and the same decay at infinity. Put
w=v−u,e(q)=21​(∇q+∇qT).
(424)
Then ∇⋅w=0 and w=0 on the sphere. The viscous dissipation satisfies
D[v]​=2μ∫D​e(u+w):e(u+w)dV=D[u]+4μ∫D​e(u):e(w)dV+2μ∫D​e(w):e(w)dV.​
(425)
For the Stokes stress
σ=−pI+2μe(u),
(426)
incompressibility of w gives
2μe(u):e(w)=σ:∇w.
(427)
The divergence theorem, the homogeneous boundary data, decay at infinity, and ∇⋅σ=0 give
∫D​σ:∇wdV=∫∂D​w⋅σndS−∫D​w⋅(∇⋅σ)dV=0.
(428)
Therefore
D[v]−D[u]=2μ∫D​e(w):e(w)dV≥0.​
(429)
This proves the Minimum-dissipation theorem for Stokes flow.
